one_liner: Multithreaded C++ tensor contraction library (TTGT over BLAS + HPTT); up to 18x over the best of Eigen Tensor, NumPy, ITensor and Tensor Toolbox.
what_it_does: TCL computes arbitrary dense tensor contractions (einsum-style, e.g. C[m,n] = A[k2,m,k1] * B[n,k2,k1]) through a single call, tcl::tensorMult(alpha, A["k2,m,k1"], B["n,k2,k1"], beta, C["m,n"]). It offers a C++ Tensor<T> class, a C interface (s/d/c/zTensorMult on raw pointers with optional outer sizes for subtensors) and a Python wrapper comparable to numpy.einsum. Column-major by default, row-major optional; float, double and complex types.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) approach: operands are permuted with HPTT, a high-performance tensor transposition library, into layouts that turn the contraction into one large GEMM on a tuned BLAS (BLIS, MKL, OpenBLAS). The speedup comes mostly from fast transpositions, so it is largest for low-arithmetic-intensity contractions where transposes dominate.
when_to_use: CPU dense tensor contractions with many index permutations (quantum chemistry, tensor networks) where Eigen Tensor or numpy.einsum is the bottleneck
Low-arithmetic-intensity contractions (small contracted dimensions), where the README reports the largest gains (up to 18x)
Multicore x86 servers with a multithreaded BLAS and pinned threads (benchmark: 2-socket Haswell-EP, 24 threads)
Python code using einsum that can call tcl.tensorMult instead
when_not_to_use: Concurrent contractions from several threads: a global MemoryBroker is not thread-safe (issue #3, assertion failure under OpenMP)
Memory-constrained runs: TTGT needs auxiliary buffers for the transposed tensors (README limitation); GETT, which avoids them, was never added
GEMM-dominated (high arithmetic intensity) contractions, where speedup falls toward 1x because any BLAS-backed library hits peak
Projects needing maintenance or GPU support: abandoned since 2019; the author points to NVIDIA cuTENSOR
Sparse or symmetric tensors: dense contractions only

integration.dependencies: HPTT, a BLAS (BLIS by default in the Makefile; MKL/OpenBLAS/ATLAS), OpenMP
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; tested with g++ 5.1.0 and icpc 17.0.2
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux as tested; Makefile builds with -march=native
integration.thread_safety: Internally multithreaded via OpenMP; not safe to call concurrently (global MemoryBroker, issue #3)

gotchas: Plain Makefile with -march=native: you must edit HPTT_ROOT/BLIS_ROOT paths, and the binary is not portable to other CPUs
Set thread affinity (KMP_AFFINITY/taskset) and OMP_NUM_THREADS, and link Python against a multithreaded BLAS, or performance suffers (README)
Index strings define the contraction; layout defaults to column-major, so row-major callers must pass useRowMajor
LGPL-3.0: static linking into closed-source code carries relinking obligations
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only general tensor-contraction entry in the category; pick it over hand-rolled transposes plus a GEMM kernel (e.g. the AVX-512 DGEMM sibling) when contractions have arbitrary index orders, and prefer T-MAC or llamafile for quantized LLM matmul instead.
verified_claims_summary: The author measured 1000 random contractions on a 2-socket Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 (Haswell-EP, 24 threads) against the fastest of Eigen Tensor, Tensor Toolbox, NumPy and ITensor for each case; TCL was faster on every case, up to 18x at low arithmetic intensity, falling toward parity as GEMM dominates. Compiler and flags for the run are not stated; first-party only.
status_note: Abandoned (last commit 2019-08-22, README says no longer maintained), LGPL-3.0; small enough to vendor but expect to fix the thread-safety bug yourself.
